Gandalf was an Istar (Wizard) dispatched to Middle-earth in the Third Age to combat the threat of Sauron [1]. Originally named Olórin in Quenya, he was accounted as the wisest of the Maiar [1]. He was known by many names during his wanderings: the Elves called him Mithrandir ("the Grey Pilgrim"), while the Men of Arnor coined the name Gandalf, which became his most common name; he was also known as Incánus in the South and Tharkûn to the Dwarves [3]. He eventually became known as not only the wisest but also the most powerful of the Istari [3].

In appearance, Gandalf was described as an old man with a pointed blue hat, a long grey cloak, a silver scarf, a long white beard, and bushy eyebrows that stuck out beyond the brim of his hat [2]. Though immortal and effectively ageless as one of the Istari, his body of flesh appeared old from the beginning [2].

reference: Gandalf is one of the Istari (Wizards), a Maia sent by the Valar to oppose Sauron. He was known as Gandalf the Grey and later returned as Gandalf the White. The Elves called him Mithrandir. He guided the Free Peoples through the War of the Ring and was reckoned the wisest of the Maiar.

response: Smaug was killed by Bard the Bowman [1][2][3][4]. Bard was a descendant of Girion, Lord of Dale [1], and he killed the dragon by shooting a Black Arrow into a vulnerable spot on Smaug's left breast [2][3]. This weakness—a bare spot in Smaug's otherwise jewel-encrusted underbelly—had been discovered earlier by the hobbit Bilbo Baggins, and the information was passed to Bard by a thrush [1][3]. user_input: What rings did the Dwarves get?
retrieved_contexts: ['. Whereas the Men who owned the nine Rings were corrupted and became the Nazgûl , the Dwarves were unaffected, save by an increase of their goldlust and hatred for anything that stood between them and what they perceived as their treasure. Crafting Dwarves were taught special skills by the Vala Aulë and spent most of their time crafting, smithying and mining in their massive underground cities. The Dwarves were some of the greatest miners ever to exist in Middle-earth. The Dwarves dug immense halls under mountains where they built their cities. Dwarven miners dug for precious minerals such as gold, iron, copper, and silver from all over mountains in Middle-earth, though the Dwarves considered coal mining degrading. In ancient times, the Dwarves found mithril in the mines of Khazad-dûm', '. The only apparent effect of the Dwarven rings was that the Dwarves became more greedy with gold lust, but they were not turned into wraiths like men. Sauron subsequently tried to recover the rings. Two he reclaimed fairly soon and four ended up in dragon hoards. Sauron did not reclaim the ring of Durin until the year TA 2845 , when he captured Thráin II . Of the Dwarves, few fought upon either side in the War of the Last Alliance ; but the kindred of Durin of Khazad-dûm fought against Sauron. Third Age In 1980 of the Third Age, after centuries of greedily digging for mithril and other minerals, the Dwarves woke a Balrog that was sleeping in the deeps of the Misty Mountains since the First Age. The Dwarves fled Khazad-dûm, which from then on was called Moria , which means "Black pit"', "Sauron gave seven Rings of Power to Dwarf lords. The Rings caused them to be wrathful and greedy for gold, but they were not brought under Sauron's domination, nor did they gain longer life. Eventually all seven Rings were destroyed or reclaimed by Sauron. One of the rings was given to Durin III, and passed down to Thrór, who gave it to his son Thráin II, father of Thorin Oakenshield. Sauron captured Thráin and took the ring from him in the dungeons of Dol Guldur.", ". This was the ring that Thráin II later carried and had taken from him when he was captured by the agents of Sauron. During the War of the Elves and Sauron the Dark Lord 's forces were on the point of overtaking and destroying the refugees and army of Elrond , when the Dwarves of Khazad-dûm sortied from the Doors of Durin and attacked Sauron's forces in the rear, giving the Elves time to escape and earning the Dark Lord's enmity. After this time the gates of Khazad-dûm were shut. In adaptations The Lord of the Rings film trilogy Durin III appears momentarily in the prologue of The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring as he receives one of the Seven Dwarf-rings"]
response:
The Dwarves received seven Rings of Power from Sauron [3]. These rings had a notable effect on the Dwarves: they increased their greed for gold and made them more wrathful, but unlike Men who received rings and became the Nazgûl, the Dwarves were not corrupted into wraiths or brought under Sauron's domination, nor did the rings extend their lifespans [1][3].

One of these seven rings was given to Durin III and became known as the ring of Durin [3][4]. This particular ring was passed down through Durin's line to Thrór, then to his son Thráin II [3]. Eventually, Sauron recaptured this ring when he captured Thráin II in TA 2845 in the dungeons of Dol Guldur [2][3][4]. Of the other rings, Sauron reclaimed two fairly soon, and four ended up in dragon hoards [2]. By the time of the War of the Ring, all seven rings had been either destroyed or reclaimed by Sauron [3].
reference: The Dwarves were given Seven Rings of Power by Sauron. Unlike the Men who received the Nine and became the Nazgûl, the Dwarves were not corrupted into wraiths; the Rings instead increased their greed for gold. Over time Sauron recovered some of the Seven and dragons consumed others.

response:
The Battle of Five Armies was a major conflict fought on and near the Lonely Mountain between the Goblins and Wargs of the Misty Mountains and Grey Mountains on one side, and the Lake-men, Elves, and Dwarves on the other [1]. The battle occurred after Thorin's quest successfully retook Erebor and Smaug was killed, but tensions arose between the Dwarves and their potential allies [3].

The goblin army was led by Bolg and attacked from the North, where a vast host had been assembled at their capital of Gundabad [1][2]. Despite the goblins' assault forcing the previously quarreling Dwarves, Elves, and Men to unite, the goblins were ultimately defeated [2]. However, the victory came at a heavy cost: Thorin Oakenshield and his nephews Fíli and Kíli were mortally wounded [2]. Beorn, chieftain of the Beornings, played a crucial role by slaying Bolg, scattering his bodyguard, and carrying the dying Thorin to safety [2].

Bilbo Baggins witnessed only part of the battle, as he was knocked unconscious early in the fighting and lay undiscovered while wearing his ring until the battle's conclusion [2].
reference: The Battle of Five Armies was fought at the Lonely Mountain (Erebor) after Smaug's death. The five armies were Dwarves, Elves, and Men against Goblins and Wargs, with the goblin host led by Bolg. Thorin Oakenshield and his nephews Fíli and Kíli were killed, and the Eagles and Beorn turned the tide for the victory of the Free Peoples.

response:
Beren and Lúthien's story is one of the most famous love stories in Middle-earth. Beren was a mortal man fleeing from Morgoth, while Lúthien (also known as Tinúviel) was the immortal princess of Doriath, daughter of the powerful Elven King Thingol and a Maia [1][4]. Their relationship faced immense obstacles: Thingol forbade their marriage and set an impossible bride price—Beren had to bring him a Silmaril from Morgoth's iron crown [1].

Despite overwhelming odds, including kidnapping by the Sons of Fëanor, the death of their ally Finrod Felagund, and a confrontation with Sauron, the couple succeeded in their quest with help from Huan, the Hound of Valinor [1]. However, Beren died immediately after completing the task [1]. Their love was so profound that Lúthien chose to become mortal to be with Beren, and they were granted a second life together in Middle-earth by the Vala Mandos [2][4]. They dwelt on Tol Galen and had a son named Dior, called Elúchil, the Heir of Thingol [2]. After the sack of Menegroth, Beren ambushed the Dwarves responsible and recovered the Nauglamír for Lúthien [2].

Their story was so meaningful to J.R.R. Tolkien that he had "Lúthien" inscribed on his wife Edith's grave marker and "Beren" on his own [3].
reference: Beren, a mortal Man, and Lúthien, the half-Maia daughter of the Elven King Thingol, fell in love. Thingol set a bride-price of a Silmaril from Morgoth's crown. They recovered a Silmaril together, but Beren died; for her love Lúthien chose to become mortal and they were granted a second life, dwelling on Tol Galen and having a son, Dior. (Corpus note: coverage comes from the Lúthien article; there is no standalone Beren article.)

["Mithril is a fictional metal found in J. R. R. Tolkien's Middle-earth writings. It is described as resembling silver, but being stronger and lighter than steel. It was used to make armour, such as the helmets of the citadel guard of Minas Tirith, and ithildin alloy, used to decorate gateways with writing visible only by starlight or moonlight. Always extremely valuable, by the end of the Third Age it was beyond price, and only a few artefacts made of it remained in use.", 'The metallurgist James Owen suggests that Mithril could be "an fcc [face-centred cubic] metal like aluminium or nickel, or possibly a bcc [body-centred cubic]" metal like titanium". Owen comments that it could form "strong, stiff, tough alloys" with those elements, suitable for "light sword blades and armour", or used as the pure element, when "it would be soft and malleable" like copper or gold. The geologist William Sarjeant, however, notes that mithril crystallises out "at so high a temperature that it is only found in veins at great depths", and proposes that it may be a native alloy of platinum with another metal, which might be palladium.', '=== Metallurgy ===
The chemist Suze Kundu describes mithril as a metal, a pure chemical element with "a range of amazing chemical and physical properties" not matched by any real metal, and many applications. Of those that approach it, titanium is light (has a low density) and strong, but it is not malleable (able to be beaten into shape) like mithril. In Kundu's view the nearest material would be a stainless steel alloy of iron with enough nano-scale carbon to make it hard.', '== Tolkien ==


=== Etymology ===
The name mithril comes from two words in Tolkien's Sindarin language—mith, meaning "grey", and ril, meaning "glitter".  The Dwarves kept their own name for the material secret.


=== Properties ===
In The Hobbit, Thorin Oakenshield described some Dwarven treasures as "coats of mail gilded and silvered and impenetrable" and "a coat of dwarf-linked rings the like of which had never been made before, for it was wrought of pure silver to the power and strength of triple steel." A little later the narrator describes "a small coat of mail, wrought for some young elf-prince long ago. It was of silver-steel which the elves call mithril".
In The Fellowship of the Ring, the wizard Gandalf explained mithril to the rest of the Fellowship in Moria:']
response:
Mithril is a fictional metal from J.R.R. Tolkien's Middle-earth that resembles silver but is stronger and lighter than steel [1]. The name comes from two Sindarin words: "mith" meaning "grey" and "ril" meaning "glitter," though the Dwarves kept their own name for it secret [4].

It was highly valued for making armor and other objects. Examples include the helmets of Minas Tirith's citadel guard and ithildin alloy used to decorate gateways [1]. In *The Hobbit*, a mithril coat is described as "silver-steel" or "pure silver to the power and strength of triple steel," making it both beautiful and nearly impenetrable [4]. By the end of the Third Age, mithril had become so rare it was beyond price, with only a few artifacts remaining in use [1].
reference: Mithril is a fictional silver-like metal in Tolkien's Middle-earth, stronger and lighter than steel. It was found and mined by the Dwarves in Moria (Khazad-dûm). It was extremely valuable; Bilbo's mithril mail shirt, later worn by Frodo, is a notable example of its use.

He first appeared in print in a 1934 poem called "The Adventures of Tom Bombadil", which included The Lord of the Rings characters Goldberry (his wife), Old Man Willow (an evil tree in his forest) and the barrow-wight, from whom he rescues the hobbits. response:
Tom Bombadil is a character in J. R. R. Tolkien's legendarium who first appeared in a 1934 poem called "The Adventures of Tom Bombadil" [1]. Tolkien invented the character in memory of his children's Dutch doll, and the Bombadil poems predated The Lord of the Rings by many years [2]. In The Lord of the Rings, Bombadil appears as a supporting character in The Fellowship of the Ring, where Frodo Baggins and company meet him in the Old Forest [3]. He is accompanied by Goldberry (his wife) and encounters Old Man Willow and the barrow-wight [1].

Tolkien described Tom as "just an invention" and "not an important person – to the narrative," though he represented "something that I feel important" related to a renunciation of control and "a delight in things for themselves without reference to yourself" [2]. Tolkien also stated that "even in a mythical Age there must be some enigmas, as there always are. Tom Bombadil is one (intentionally)" [4]. In an earlier 1937 letter, Tolkien called Tom the spirit of the vanishing landscapes of Oxfordshire and Berkshire, though this was before The Lord of the Rings was written [4].

Bombadil has been omitted from most adaptations of The Lord of the Rings, including radio adaptations, the 1978 animated film, and Peter Jackson's film trilogy, as nonessential to the story [3].
reference: Tom Bombadil is an enigmatic character in The Lord of the Rings who lives in the Old Forest with his wife Goldberry. He is unaffected by the One Ring: it does not turn him invisible and has no power over him. Tolkien deliberately left his true nature and origin unexplained.
